YAML parses with js-yaml, every `run:` block passes `bash -n`, and I ran the new check and rename steps against fake `dist/` and `builds/` trees to confirm they pass on good output and fail on each missing piece.

## What changed in the workflow

**Build job, two new steps between `electron-builder` and the upload:**

1. `Name the files the way the update feed does` — renames any file in `dist/` containing a space to the dashed form (`Crew Setup 0.1.0.exe` → `Crew-Setup-0.1.0.exe`). See the finding below, this one was not in the brief and OTA on Windows does not work without it.
2. `Check the update files are there` — per platform, fails the build if the yml is missing, if there are not exactly two mac zips on disk, if `latest-mac.yml` does not list two zips, if there is no dmg or no exe, or if no blockmap was built.

**`upload-artifact` path** widened from `dist/*.dmg` + `dist/*.exe` to `dist/*.dmg`, `dist/*-mac.zip`, `dist/*.exe`, `dist/*.blockmap`, `dist/latest-mac.yml`, `dist/latest.yml`. `if-no-files-found: error` kept.

**Release job**: added `defaults.run.shell: bash`, and the script now builds an explicit asset array (`*.dmg`, `*-mac.zip`, `*.exe`, `*.blockmap`, both ymls) under `nullglob`, checks exactly one `latest-mac.yml` and one `latest.yml` arrived, and passes that array to `gh release create`/`gh release upload` instead of `builds/*/*`. Still `--publish never` plus one release job.

## Findings

**1. What GitHubProvider fetches.** `getLatestVersion` reads `https://github.com/JamelHammoud/crew/releases.atom` for release notes, and separately `getLatestTagName` hits `https://github.com/JamelHammoud/crew/releases/latest` with `Accept: application/json` to get `tag_name`. That endpoint is GitHub's own "latest" pointer, which excludes drafts and prereleases, so with the default `allowPrerelease: false` drafts and prereleases are ignored. With `allowPrerelease: true` it walks the atom feed instead and prereleases are eligible (drafts never appear in the atom feed either way). It then downloads one channel file from `releases/download/<tag>/<name>`: `getChannelFilePrefix()` in `Provider.js:30` returns `-mac` on darwin and `""` on win32, so macOS asks for `latest-mac.yml` and Windows for `latest.yml`. Every other asset comes from the `files[].url` list inside that yml, resolved against the same `releases/download/<tag>/` base with spaces replaced by dashes (`GitHubProvider.js:181`). `MacUpdater` filters that list by arch (`arm64` in the filename) and picks the zip, explicitly excluding pkg and dmg. Blockmaps are never named in the yml: `Provider.getBlockMapFiles` derives them as `<file url>.blockmap` for both the new and the previous version, so they must sit on the release under exactly the yml's filename plus `.blockmap`. `gh release create` with no `--draft`/`--prerelease` is correct here, do not add either flag.

**2. One `latest-mac.yml` for both arches, confirmed.** `getUpdateInfoFileName` (`app-builder-lib/out/publish/updateInfoBuilder.js:51`) appends an arch suffix only on Linux, so x64 and arm64 both target `dist/latest-mac.yml`. Both arches push a task for that same path, and `writeUpdateInfoFiles` (line 154) keys tasks by file path plus publish config and merges with `existingTask.info.files.push(...task.info.files)`, writing once at the end of the run. So the single `--mac --x64 --arm64` invocation produces one yml listing four files: both zips first (they are sorted zip-first) then both dmgs. Nothing overwrites. The caveat is that this merge only holds inside one electron-builder process, so splitting mac into two invocations later would silently leave you with one arch. The new check step asserts the count is two, so that regression fails the build.

**3. `if-no-files-found: error` alone was not the guarantee you wanted.** It fires only when the entire multi-line path set matches nothing, not per line. On the mac runner a missing `latest-mac.yml` would still leave the dmg matching, so the upload would succeed and ship an unusable release. That is why the explicit check step exists, and it is what actually enforces point 3.

**4. Signing and notarization.** Yes, an unsigned build silently produces a release mac clients cannot install. In `macPackager.js:176`, when no identity is found and `forceCodeSigning` is unset (it is unset in `package.json`), `reportError` logs a warning rather than throwing (`codeSign/macCodeSign.js:77`) and `sign()` returns `false`. The build then goes on to produce the dmg, both zips and a complete `latest-mac.yml`, the workflow goes green, the release is created, and Squirrel.Mac rejects the bundle at install time. And notarization is invoked, but only on the signed path: `notarizeIfProvided` is called at `macPackager.js:289`, after the identity gate, so if signing was skipped it is never reached and you get no warning about notarization at all. With `CSC_LINK` present, `mac.notarize` is unset in `package.json` which means "not false", and `getNotarizeOptions` picks up `APPLE_ID` + `APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD` + `APPLE_TEAM_ID` and runs `notarytool`, throwing `InvalidConfigurationError` if any one of the three is missing. So notarization is real when the certificate is there. I changed nothing about signing. If you want an unsigned mac build to fail loudly rather than ship, the fix is `"forceCodeSigning": true` in `build.mac`, which is a package.json change and outside what I was asked to touch.

**One thing that differed from the brief.** Windows asset names do not match the update feed without a rename. The default nsis filename is `${productName} Setup ${version}.${ext}` (`NsisTarget.js:99`), so the file on disk is `Crew Setup 0.1.0.exe`, but `latest.yml` records the GitHub-safe name `Crew-Setup-0.1.0.exe` (`computeSafeArtifactNameIfNeeded` replaces spaces with dashes, `platformPackager.js:585`). electron-builder's own publisher does that rename on upload, but `--publish never` means it never runs, and `gh release upload` uses the literal basename, which GitHub then stores with spaces turned into dots (`Crew.Setup.0.1.0.exe`). electron-updater would request `Crew-Setup-0.1.0.exe` and get a 404, along with its blockmap. The rename step is what closes that gap. Mac names have no spaces, so the step is a no-op there and I left it unconditional rather than adding a branch.

I need to refine the conditional logic for showing the buttons—when in reading mode, the changes button should disappear even if there's a base version. I'll update the condition from just `base` to `base && !reading` in both the wrapper and the button itself. To keep it cleaner, I could extract this as a variable like `const changes = !!base && !reading` and use that throughout, though I'm still deciding where to define it.

Looking at the `dirty` state, there's an issue: it currently depends on `editable`, which becomes false while reading. This means if I make unsaved edits and switch to preview, the Save and Discard buttons vanish even though the preview shows the unsaved text—I can't save without flipping back to edit mode. Instead, I should base `dirty` on whether the file is writable, independent of the reading state. I'm restructuring the logic so `writable` checks the file validity, `reading` determines preview mode, `editable` combines both, and `dirty` stays available as long as the file is writable. This way the save controls remain accessible while previewing unsaved changes, and the discard function will handle the null editor reference gracefully by just resetting the caret position.

The launcher passes the folder path resolved from the execution location, the request as a command-line flag, and sets the working directory accordingly—I'm noting the `/private/tmp` versus `/tmp` difference on macOS from `process.cwd()`. Now I need to check whether Electron will accept the custom `--crew-open=` flag; Electron forwards unknown arguments to `process.argv` and Chromium might warn but that's expected behavior.

In development mode with `electron-vite dev`, command-line arguments don't matter anyway. After cleaning up the probe files, I'll add documentation to AGENTS.md—specifically a new section called "The crew command" positioned right after "Where a crew lives" since it covers how to open a project. I'll write it in the house style with plain sentences explaining what the command does, how it gets added to PATH, which Crew instance it opens, and why the request travels as a single JSON-encoded flag that gets cleaned by `cleanOpenRequest`.

Now I'm drafting the actual section for the docs, starting with what `crew` does in a terminal and how `bin/crew.mjs` works as a standalone script with no build step or dependencies.

The command takes several options: `--name` for who you are, `--in-project` and `--in-app` to specify where the crew lives, `--share` and `--no-share` for access control, and `--join <link>` to connect to someone else's crew. The `--help` and `--version` flags work as expected without opening anything.

Once a project has been opened, the options are remembered and won't change if you pass them again. The command packages everything into a single `--crew-open=` flag with JSON data rather than repeating all the individual flags, since the app shouldn't have to relearn what those flags mean. The `cleanOpenRequest` function in the shared CLI code extracts just what matters—the folder, name, the two location answers, and the link—and discards the rest, keeping the flag's logic entirely in the command layer.

When a window opens for a folder, it takes priority over resuming the previous session, since both would race otherwise. The renderer handles the request by checking the name and project status: if there's no name, it goes to the naming screen; if the project is unknown, it asks the setup question; if it's known, it opens directly. The request gets cleared after being used so leaving the session doesn't loop back to the folder the terminal requested.

Which Crew launches depends on the `CREW_APP` environment variable if set, otherwise the installed app, or finally the one built locally—and `yarn build` is what makes that last option available. The CLI will error saying "no Crew to open. Install the app, or point CREW_APP at one" if none of those exist. Each run is its own instance, so multiple Crew folders can coexist, and multiple windows on one folder were already supported. The CLI gets on PATH through `npm link` in the checkout or a symlink of the executable, but nothing installs it automatically.

I'm wondering if the error message should mention building as an option, since that's how someone would create a Crew to open in the first place.

+ - Taking a place off the list is a right click on it. A button fading in over the arrow was a second control standing on top of a row that has one thing to press, and it cost the arrow that says where the row goes. A project and a crew somebody invited you to both go, by folder and by link, so no row on the list is one you are stuck with.
+ 
+ ## The crew command
+ 
+ `crew` in a terminal opens a crew on the folder you are standing in. `bin/crew.mjs` is the whole of it: plain node, no dependencies and no build step, so the one command works from a checkout and from the installed app alike.
+ 
+ - The folder is the one you are in unless you name another, and a relative one is worked out from where the command was run rather than from wherever the app happens to start. `--name` is who you are, `--in-project` and `--in-app` are the two answers to where the crew lives, `--share` and `--no-share` are who can reach it, and `--join <link>` joins somebody else's crew with this folder as the place your agents work. `--help` and `--version` answer for themselves and open nothing.
+ - Where a crew lives and who can reach it is the host's own, so `--join` is refused either of them rather than quietly ignoring them. Everything else is the same question the app asks the first time a project is opened and remembers from then on, which is why giving it again on a folder you have opened before changes nothing.
+ - What the command worked out rides in one flag, `--crew-open=` with the request as JSON, rather than as the row of flags the app would then have to learn the meaning of a second time. The command owns what its own words mean and the app only says whether it can use them: `cleanOpenRequest` in `src/shared/cli.ts` keeps the folder, the name, the two answers and the link and drops the rest, so nothing on a command line can reach further into the app than that. A plain node script cannot import the app's TypeScript, so the flag is the one thing written down twice, and `tests/crew-cli.test.ts` sends a real request through both halves and holds them to agreeing.
+ - A window launched for a folder opens that folder, so main leaves the last session where it is while a request is waiting. Resumed as well, the two would race and the one that lost would be the folder somebody just asked for.
+ - The renderer acts on it rather than main, because the name you go by lives in the window and the one question a project is asked is a screen in `Home`. `follow` walks the same path a press on a row does: no name goes to the name screen and comes back to the request when it has one, a project the app has never opened goes to the question, and a known one opens straight away. The request is handed over once and cleared, or leaving a session would land you back in the folder the terminal asked for.
+ - Which Crew it opens is `CREW_APP` if that is set, then the installed app, then the one built in this checkout. Nothing is looked up on PATH, since the command is called `crew` too and a Linux install puts its own `crew` there.
+ - Every run is an app of its own, which is what lets the command open two folders as two crews. Nothing here takes a lock, so several windows on one folder is still supported.
+ - It reaches PATH with `npm link` in the checkout, or a symlink of `bin/crew.mjs` into somewhere on PATH. Nothing installs it for you, and the `bin` entry in `package.json` is what npm reads.
